decks.title: Absorption by Roots — Part 1: Diffusion, osmosis and plasmolysis
goals: Distinguish imbibition, diffusion and osmosis with examples, and explain osmotic pressure
Describe the potassium permanganate, thistle funnel and potato osmoscope experiments
Explain turgidity, flaccidity and plasmolysis, and predict what happens to cells in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions

slides.heading: Absorption by Roots and the Ascent of Sap
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the physical processes that move water into and out of cells.

visual.alt: Flow: imbibition, diffusion, osmosis, then turgor and plasmolysis

slides.narration: A plant cannot drink. Yet a tall tree moves hundreds of litres of water from soil to leaves every day. It all begins with simple physical processes that move water into and out of cells.

slides.heading: Imbibition
slides.body_md: **Imbibition** is the absorption of water by **dry solid materials**, which then **swell**.

visual.alt: Table of three examples of imbibition

slides.narration: Dry seeds, raisins and wood all soak up water and swell. This is imbibition. It needs no membrane and no energy. It is the first step when a seed begins to germinate.

slides.heading: Diffusion
slides.body_md: **Diffusion** is the movement of molecules from a region of **higher** concentration to **lower** concentration until they are evenly spread.

slides.heading: Hypotonic, isotonic, hypertonic

visual.alt: Table of hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions with water movement and the state of the cell

slides.narration: Compare the outside solution with the cell sap. If it is weaker, water enters and the cell swells. If it is equal, nothing changes. If it is stronger, water leaves and the cell shrinks. Osmotic pressure is higher in stronger solutions.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: potato strips
slides.body_md: Equal potato strips in sugar solutions for two hours (imagined data).
bullets: Step 1: percentage change = change in mass divided by starting mass, times one hundred.
Step 2: find where the change is zero.
Step 3: that solution is isotonic with the cell sap.

visual.alt: Worked table of percentage change in mass: plus twelve, plus six, zero, minus six and minus twelve as sugar strength rises

slides.narration: Strips in weak solutions gained mass, and those in strong solutions lost it. In the zero point two molar solution there was no change, so the potato cell sap has about that strength.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Imbibition: dry solids absorb water and swell.
Diffusion: molecules spread from high to low concentration.
Osmosis: water crosses a selectively permeable membrane towards the stronger solution.
Hypotonic → turgid; isotonic → no change; hypertonic → plasmolysed.

visual.alt: Summary table of whether each process needs a membrane

slides.narration: To recap. Imbibition swells dry things. Diffusion spreads molecules. Osmosis moves water through a membrane towards the stronger solution. Cells swell in weak solutions and shrink in strong ones.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always mention the **selectively permeable membrane** in osmosis.
Say **water** moves in osmosis, never "sugar" or "salt".
In experiments, name the **control** and say what it shows.
Plasmolysis is the **state**; exosmosis is the **process**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Mention the membrane whenever you explain osmosis. Remember that only water moves. Always identify the control in an experiment. And keep the words for the state and the process separate.

slides.heading: The root hair

slides.narration: Roots are shaped for their job. Countless root hairs give a huge surface. Thin walls and strong sap draw water in. And branching roots reach water spread through a large volume of soil.

slides.narration: Minerals enter as dissolved ions. Some simply diffuse in. But roots often hold more ions than the soil, so they must pump them in against the gradient. That active transport uses energy from respiration, which needs oxygen in the soil.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: waterlogged field
slides.body_md: After a week of flooding, a farmer’s maize plants turn pale and stop growing. Explain.
bullets: Step 1: flooding drives **air** out of the soil.
Step 2: roots get little **oxygen**, so **respiration** slows.
Step 3: less energy means less **active uptake** of minerals, so the leaves turn pale.

visual.alt: Flow: flooded soil, little oxygen, less respiration, fewer minerals absorbed

slides.narration: Link the steps. No air in the soil means little oxygen for the roots. Without oxygen, respiration slows and there is little energy to pump minerals in. Short of minerals such as nitrogen, the plant turns pale.

slides.heading: The ascent of sap

rows: Roots push water up from below; seen as sap oozing from a cut stump
Evaporation from leaves pulls water up the xylem
Water molecules attract each other, so the column stays unbroken
Water clings to the xylem walls

slides.narration: Water rises in the xylem by a push and a pull. Root pressure pushes a little from below. Transpiration pull from the leaves does most of the work. Cohesion keeps the thin water column unbroken, and adhesion holds it to the vessel walls.

notes.title: Absorption by Roots and the Ascent of Sap — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Imbibition, diffusion and osmosis
sections.body_md:
- **Imbibition:** absorption of water by **dry solid materials** (seeds, raisins, wood), which swell. No membrane, no energy.
- **Diffusion:** movement of molecules from a region of **higher** to **lower** concentration until evenly spread (scent in a room; a **potassium permanganate** crystal colouring still water).
- **Osmosis:** movement of **water** molecules through a **selectively permeable membrane** from a **dilute** (hypotonic) solution to a **concentrated** (hypertonic) one. **Endosmosis** = water entering a cell; **exosmosis** = water leaving.
- **Osmotic pressure:** the pressure needed to prevent water entering a solution by osmosis; greater for **stronger** solutions.

**Experiments**
- **Thistle funnel:** sugar solution in a funnel closed with **parchment**, dipped in water → level in the stem **rises** (endosmosis). Control: funnel with water — no rise.
- **Potato osmoscope:** hollowed potato with strong sugar solution stood in water → level inside **rises**; potato cells act as the membrane. Control: empty cup (or boiled potato — cells dead, no osmosis).

sections.heading: 2. Turgidity, flaccidity and plasmolysis
sections.body_md:
| Outside solution | Water movement | State of cell |
|---|---|---|
| **Hypotonic** (weaker than cell sap) | Enters (endosmosis) | **Turgid** — cytoplasm pressed against the wall |
| **Isotonic** (equal) | No net movement | No change; a cell that has lost some water stays **flaccid** (limp) |
| **Hypertonic** (stronger) | Leaves (exosmosis) | **Plasmolysed** — cytoplasm shrinks away from the wall |

**Deplasmolysis:** a plasmolysed cell placed in water soon enough regains water and becomes turgid.

**Importance of turgidity:** keeps soft stems and leaves **firm**; opens **stomata**; helps **growth**. Loss of turgor → **wilting**.

**Everyday examples:** salt or sugar preserves pickles and jams (microbes are plasmolysed); excess fertiliser or salt makes plants wilt; sprinkling water keeps vegetables crisp.

Limp; no pressure on the wall.
Shrinking of the cytoplasm away from the cell wall due to exosmosis.
Recovery of a plasmolysed cell in water.

sections.heading: 3. The root hair
sections.body_md:
A **root hair** is a long, thin tubular outgrowth of a **single epidermal cell** in the root hair zone.

**Structure:** thin **cell wall** (freely permeable), **cell membrane** (selectively permeable), **cytoplasm** lining the cell, **nucleus**, and a large **vacuole** of cell sap that extends into the hair.

**Adaptations of roots for absorbing water**
- Thousands of root hairs give an **enormous surface area**.
- Root hairs have **thin walls** and **no cuticle**.
- Cell sap is **more concentrated** than soil water, so water enters by **osmosis**.
- Hairs grow **between soil particles**, in contact with the water film.

key_terms.definition_md: A tubular outgrowth of one epidermal cell of the root.

sections.heading: 4. Absorption of water and minerals
sections.body_md:
**Path of water:** soil water → **root hair** → **cortex** → **endodermis** → **pericycle** → **xylem**. Water moves cell to cell by **osmosis**, because each inner cell has slightly more concentrated sap.

**Minerals** are absorbed as **ions**:
- **Passive absorption:** by **diffusion**, down the concentration gradient; no energy.
- **Active absorption:** **against** the concentration gradient, using **energy (ATP)** from respiration. It needs **oxygen** in the soil, so waterlogged soil reduces mineral uptake.

key_terms.definition_md: Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy.
Movement down a concentration gradient without energy.

sections.heading: 5. Ascent of sap
sections.body_md:
**Ascent of sap** is the upward movement of water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves through the **xylem**.
- **Root pressure:** pressure in the roots that pushes water up a short distance; seen as **sap oozing** from a freshly cut stump.
- **Transpiration pull:** evaporation of water from leaves creates a **suction** that pulls the water column up — the **main force** in tall trees.
- **Cohesion:** attraction between **water molecules**, which keeps the column **continuous**.
- **Adhesion:** attraction between water and the **walls of xylem vessels**.

**Experiment:** a balsam shoot in water coloured with **red ink or eosin** shows red streaks in the stem; a cross-section shows only the **xylem** stained.

Pressure developed in roots that pushes water up.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying salt or sugar moves in osmosis (only **water** does).
- Calling imbibition "osmosis".
- Drawing a root hair as many cells or with a cuticle.
- Saying root pressure lifts water to the top of tall trees.
- Mixing up plasmolysis (state) and exosmosis (process).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a process, or an odd one out with its category.
- 2 marks: two differences or reasons, each matched point for point.
- 3 marks: an experiment (set-up, observation, conclusion) or a labelled diagram (outline, key parts, labels).

questions.stem_md: A solution that is more concentrated than the cell sap, so that the cell loses water to it, is called
questions.solution_md: A stronger outside solution is hypertonic and draws water out of the cell — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A farmer adds far too much fertiliser around young plants, and they wilt even though the soil is moist. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: the roots absorbed too much water and burst
the soil water became hypertonic, so water moved out of the root cells

questions.solution_md: Concentrated soil solution draws water out of root cells (exosmosis), causing plasmolysis and wilting — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Why do salted mango pieces in a pickle not rot quickly?

options.text_md: Strong salt draws water out of bacterial cells by osmosis, killing or stopping them
Salt adds oxygen that kills bacteria
Salt makes the mango cells turgid

questions.solution_md: Salt makes a hypertonic medium; microbes lose water and cannot grow — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A plasmolysed cell can usually be restored by placing it in water soon afterwards.
questions.solution_md: True. If not left too long, water re-enters and the cell becomes turgid again — deplasmolysis.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Herbaceous plants stand upright when well watered.

**Reason (R):** Turgid cells press against one another and give support to soft stems and leaves.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and turgor pressure is what keeps soft plant parts firm and upright — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the swelling back of a plasmolysed cell when it is placed in water.

answer.model_answer_md: **Deplasmolysis.**

questions.solution_md: Deplasmolysis.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the limp state of a plant cell that has lost some water and exerts no pressure on its wall.

answer.model_answer_md: **Flaccidity** (the cell is flaccid).

questions.solution_md: Flaccid.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: sprinkling a lot of common salt on lawn weeds kills them.

answer.model_answer_md: Salt makes the soil water **hypertonic**; the weed cells **lose water** by exosmosis, become **plasmolysed** and die.

questions.solution_md: Exosmosis and plasmolysis.

questions.stem_md: Predict what happens to a plant cell placed in (a) a hypotonic solution and (b) an isotonic solution. Give a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) It becomes **turgid**: the outside is weaker, so water **enters** by osmosis. (b) It shows **no change**: concentrations are **equal**, so there is no net movement of water.

questions.solution_md: Turgid; no change.

questions.stem_md: Draw neat, labelled diagrams of a turgid cell and a plasmolysed cell. Label the cell wall, cytoplasm and vacuole in each.

answer.model_answer_md: Turgid cell: **cytoplasm pressed against the cell wall**, a **large vacuole** in the centre. Plasmolysed cell: the **cytoplasm shrunk away** from the wall into a small mass, **small vacuole**, a **gap** between wall and cytoplasm filled with outside solution.

questions.solution_md: Two labelled cells.

questions.stem_md: A root hair is

options.text_md: a long, thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell of the root
a branch of the root with many cells
a hair-like part of the root cap
a xylem vessel that grows into the soil

questions.solution_md: Each root hair is an extension of one epidermal cell — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The main advantage of the thousands of root hairs on a young root is that they

options.text_md: make the root heavier to anchor it
greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water

questions.solution_md: More surface area means more water and minerals can be absorbed — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the diagram of a root hair, which letter marks the part whose sap is more concentrated than the soil water, so that water enters by osmosis?
questions.solution_md: E is the large vacuole of cell sap. A is the cell wall, C the nucleus and F a soil particle — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Root hairs have a thick waxy cuticle to protect them from the soil.
questions.solution_md: False. Root hairs have no cuticle; their wall is thin so that water can enter easily.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the zone of a young root that bears root hairs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Root hair zone** (zone of absorption).

questions.solution_md: Root hair zone.

questions.stem_md: Give two features of a root hair that make it suited for absorbing water.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It is **long and thin**, with a **large surface area** in close contact with soil water.
2. Its **cell wall is thin** and its **sap is more concentrated** than soil water, so water enters by **osmosis**.

questions.solution_md: Surface area; thin wall; concentrated sap; no cuticle.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a single full-grown root hair. Label the cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm and vacuole.

answer.model_answer_md: An epidermal cell with a **long tubular outgrowth** among soil particles; a thin **cell wall** outside the **cell membrane**; **cytoplasm** lining the cell; a **nucleus** near the base or moving into the hair; a large **vacuole** of cell sap filling the hair.

questions.solution_md: Root hair with five labels.

marking_scheme.step: Outline of cell with long hair

questions.stem_md: Give reason: seedlings transplanted with a ball of soil around their roots wilt less.

answer.model_answer_md: The soil ball **protects the root hairs** from damage, so the seedling can keep **absorbing water**.

questions.solution_md: Root hairs intact.

questions.stem_md: Which is the correct path of water from the soil into a root?

options.text_md: Root hair → cortex → endodermis → pericycle → xylem

questions.solution_md: Water passes inwards from the root hair across the cortex, endodermis and pericycle into the xylem — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A root takes up potassium ions even though there are more potassium ions inside its cells than in the soil. This uptake is by

options.text_md: active transport, using energy from respiration

questions.solution_md: Movement against a concentration gradient needs energy — active transport, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Plants in waterlogged soil often take up fewer minerals. The most likely reason is that

options.text_md: roots get little oxygen, so respiration and active transport slow down

questions.solution_md: Active uptake needs energy from aerobic respiration; waterlogged soil is short of air — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Minerals are absorbed by roots only by diffusion.

**Reason (R):** Active transport moves ions against their concentration gradient using energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: minerals are also taken up actively, often against the gradient. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between passive and active absorption of minerals by roots.

answer.model_answer_md: **Passive:** ions move **down** their concentration gradient by **diffusion**, with **no energy** from the cell. **Active:** ions move **against** the gradient, using **energy (ATP)** from respiration and carrier proteins.

questions.solution_md: Gradient and energy.

questions.stem_md: Explain how water moves from the root hair across the cortex to the xylem.

answer.model_answer_md: Water entering the root hair makes its sap **more dilute** than the next cortex cell, so water passes on by **osmosis**. Each cell further **inwards** has slightly **stronger sap**, so water moves **cell to cell** until it reaches the **xylem**.

questions.solution_md: Osmosis along a gradient.

questions.stem_md: Before entering the xylem, water crosses a single layer of cells called the ______ and then the pericycle.
questions.solution_md: Endodermis.

questions.stem_md: The upward movement of water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves is called
questions.solution_md: Ascent of sap takes place through the xylem — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a tall tree, the main force that lifts water to the top is
questions.solution_md: Evaporation from leaves creates a pull on the continuous water column — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The column of water in the xylem does not break even when pulled from above because water molecules
questions.solution_md: Cohesion holds the water column together; adhesion holds it to the xylem walls — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When a well-watered potted balsam stem is cut just above the soil, sap oozes from the cut stump for some time. This shows
questions.solution_md: The roots push water up from below even without leaves — root pressure, option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Water and minerals move up the stem through the phloem.
questions.solution_md: False. They move up through the xylem; phloem carries food.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Water rises to the top of tall trees mainly by transpiration pull.

**Reason (R):** Root pressure alone is large enough to push water to the top of the tallest trees.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: root pressure is small and can lift water only a short way — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the attraction between water molecules and the walls of the xylem vessels.

answer.model_answer_md: **Adhesion.**

questions.solution_md: Adhesion.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Root pressure, Cohesion, Transpiration pull, Plasmolysis.

answer.model_answer_md: **Plasmolysis**; the others are **forces that help the ascent of sap**.

questions.solution_md: Plasmolysis is loss of water from a cell.

questions.stem_md: Explain how transpiration pull, cohesion and adhesion together raise water in a tall tree.

answer.model_answer_md: Water **evaporating** from leaves pulls on the water in the xylem (**transpiration pull**). **Cohesion** keeps the thin water column **unbroken**, and **adhesion** to the vessel walls stops it **slipping down**, so the whole column is drawn up.

questions.solution_md: Pull plus cohesion and adhesion.

questions.stem_md: Describe an experiment to show that water is conducted upwards through the xylem.

answer.model_answer_md: Place a leafy **balsam shoot** in water coloured with **red ink (or eosin)** and keep it in light for a few hours. **Red streaks** appear in the stem and veins. A thin **cross-section** of the stem shows that only the **xylem** of each vascular bundle is stained red, so water moves up through the **xylem**.

questions.solution_md: Coloured water; cross-section; xylem stained.

questions.stem_md: Study the experiment and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md:
Neha closed the wide mouth of a thistle funnel with a piece of parchment paper, filled it with strong sugar solution and dipped it in a beaker of water. She marked the level in the stem and read it every 30 minutes:

| Time (min) | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rise in level (mm) | 0 | 6 | 11 | 15 | 18 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Osmosis** (endosmosis).

**(b)** It acts as a **selectively permeable membrane**: water passes, sugar does not.

**(c)** 7 mm

**(d)** As water entered, the sugar solution became **more dilute**, so the **difference in concentration** between the funnel and the beaker **fell** and osmosis **slowed**.

**(e)** An identical funnel filled with **water instead of sugar solution**; its level should **not rise**, showing that the rise was due to the **sugar solution**.

**(f)** The level in the stem would **fall**, because water would move **out** of the funnel into the **stronger** sugar solution in the beaker (exosmosis).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Osmosis.

**(b)** Selectively permeable.

**(c)** Second hour: 18 − 11 = 7 mm (first hour 11 mm).

**(d)** Smaller concentration difference.

questions.passage_md:
To find the strength of potato cell sap, Ms Fernandes weighed five equal potato strips, placed each in a different sugar solution for two hours, and weighed them again.

| Sugar solution (M) | Mass at start (g) | Mass after 2 hours (g) |
|---|---|---|

answer.model_answer_md:

**(d)** The cells are **plasmolysed**: water left them by **exosmosis** and the cytoplasm **shrank away** from the walls; the strip is limp. In water, water would **re-enter** and the cells would become **turgid** again (**deplasmolysis**), if they are still alive.

**(e)** To make it a **fair test**, so only the **sugar concentration** differed.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: A gardener cut a leafy balsam shoot and stood it in water coloured with red ink. After three hours red lines could be seen in the stem and leaf veins. On a hot, windy afternoon the red colour reached the leaves faster than on a cool, still evening.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **xylem**.

**(b)** **Ascent of sap.**

**(c)** Heat and wind **increase transpiration** from the leaves, which **increases the transpiration pull** on the water column, so water rises **faster**.

**(d)** **Cohesion:** water molecules **attract one another**, so the water forms a **continuous column** that does not break when pulled from above. **Adhesion:** water molecules **cling to the walls** of the narrow xylem vessels, which **supports** the column and helps it rise.

**(e)** **Root pressure** is the pressure that **pushes water up** from the roots, seen when sap oozes from a cut stem. It is **small**, enough to lift water only a **few metres**, not to the top of tall trees.

**(f)** Light **opens the stomata** and increases **transpiration**, so the coloured water rises faster.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Xylem.

**(b)** Ascent of sap.

**(c)** More transpiration pull.

**(d)** Cohesion and adhesion.

**(e)** Small push from roots.

**(f)** More transpiration.

questions.stem_md: A student repeats the potato osmoscope experiment with a potato that was first boiled. The level of sugar solution in the cup does not rise because

options.text_md: boiling killed the cells, so their membranes are no longer selectively permeable
the water in the beaker evaporated

questions.solution_md: Osmosis needs living cell membranes; boiled cells let both water and sugar pass freely — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Leaves of a plant wilt on a hot afternoon when the cells lose turgor faster than water is absorbed.
questions.solution_md: True. When water loss exceeds uptake, cells become flaccid and the leaves droop.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why a seedling pulled out of dry soil without care wilts soon after it is transplanted.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its delicate **root hairs are torn off**, so the **surface area** for absorbing water is greatly reduced.
2. Its leaves continue to **lose water by transpiration**, so water loss exceeds uptake and the cells lose **turgor**.

questions.solution_md: Root hairs damaged; transpiration continues.
